newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania revises budget to meet IMF demands.
newsitem.headline: Romania revises budget to meet IMF demands.

text.p: Romania took a key step towards securing fresh IMF credits on Wednesday, approving a revised 1997 budget which kept the deficit at a level directed by the Fund, government ministers said.
Finance Minister Mircea Ciumara said the budget had received approval in principle from the centrist cabinet after a session on Tuesday night extending well past midnight.

He said the meeting had channelled more funds to the social sphere while other ministers had agreed to reductions to meet the International Monetary Fund's demand to maintain the deficit at 4.5 percent of gross domestic product.

"The budget has been approved and the deficit stays at 4.5 percent of GDP," Ciumara said by telephone. "There have been increased allocations for the Health, Education and Labour Ministries. All others have been subject to cuts."

Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea, who heads a coalition of Christian Democrats, Social Democrats and members of Romania's Hungarian minority, held a fresh round of talks through the afternoon with the IMF's chief negotiator.
Government spokesman Eugen Serbanescu said the talks would settle details of the memorandum the government will submit to the IMF for of the second of five $86 million loan tranches.
The final version of the memorandum and the budget text would be discussed at a new cabinet meeting later in the day and subsequently made public, he said.

President Emil Constantinescu last week said he might shuffle or dismiss the cabinet unless reforms proceeded more quickly. He told a gathering of war veterans on Wednesday that without changes "we will be poorer and hungrier than before".

The IMF's chief negotiator, Poul Thomsen, has made no comment on how the Fund views the government's record in implementing reforms launched after the centrists ended seven years of rule ex-communists in last year's elections.

Ciumara said budget calculations had taken into account lost revenue equivalent to $47 million for wage indexation agreed with trade unions and a further $82 million for maintaining subsidised electricity prices through the winter.
"I think the IMF is happy," he said. "They are now discussing micro-economic reform. If this influences the budget, we will make changes but I hope it won't."

Ciumara had said on Tuesday, before the budget was approved, that the government would not guarantee for this year a deal to build nearly 100 combat helicopters in Romania with a U.S. firm as part of efforts to limit foreign borrowing.
Further unexpected constraints came from flooding which damaged houses in various regions and threatened what had earlier been forecast to be a bumper grain harvest.
Approval of a new budget was one of the principal IMF demands for release of the second credit under a $430 million 13-month standby arrangement.
Others included renewed efforts to bring down monthly inflation, due to fall below two percent in July after hitting 30 percent in March owing to price liberalisation.
The pace of privatisation and restructuring inefficient communist-era enterprises were also key issues.
Ciumara, who has previously admitted that revenue from sell-offs was low, said he hoped "privatisation will accelerate in the months ahead...I am relying a great deal on this money."

Ministers have also been critical of delays in restructuring or shutting down inefficient plants and farms. The government earlier this year issued a list of enterprises to be closed but little has been done to carry out the plan.
